query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coating—specifically an alloy in the AlCoCrFeNi (or similar) family—onto a copper (Cu) substrate using controlled sputtering conditions will produce a strongly adherent, wear‐resistant surface layer due to the formation of a thin interdiffused interface that enhances metallurgical bonding.
generation.material_initial_state: A Cu matrix substrate with a smooth surface and no additional protective coating.
generation.intervention: Deposit an HEA coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi-based composition) using physical vapor deposition (sputtering) under controlled atmosphere while varying the substrate temperature.
generation.conditions: Deposition performed under a controlled inert atmosphere with substrate temperatures adjusted to promote limited interdiffusion without overheating the Cu substrate.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanometer‐scale interfacial layer formed by partial atomic interdiffusion between the Cu substrate and the HEA coating.
generation.mechanism: Optimized deposition conditions enable a controlled interdiffusion at the interface, leading to metallurgical bonding (and possibly formation of transitional phases) that anchors the hard, wear‐resistant HEA layer to the Cu matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Cu substrate with the sputtered HEA coating will exhibit improved adhesion (as measured by scratch and indentation tests) and enhanced wear resistance compared to uncoated Cu, though the exact improvement is subject to optimization of deposition parameters.
generation.baseline: A Cu substrate without any coating shows lower wear resistance and poor performance in surface protection applications.
generation.boundary: If the deposition temperature is too high or the HEA composition is not optimized for compatibility with Cu, excessive interdiffusion or brittle intermetallic compound formation could occur, deteriorating adhesion and overall performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal deposition temperature range and composition balance for minimizing detrimental reactions at the Cu/HEA interface need to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple Cu substrates with sputtered HEA coatings using a range of substrate temperatures and deposition parameters. Assess the interfacial microstructure via SEM/EDS and measure adhesion using standardized scratch and indentation tests. Compare wear resistance under controlled sliding wear tests between coated and uncoated Cu samples.
measurements: Scratch test critical load for coating delamination
SEM/EDS analysis of interfacial layer composition and thickness
Wear rate measurements during sliding wear tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated Cu samples do not show statistically significant improvements in adhesion and wear resistance relative to the uncoated control, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal an interdiffused interfacial layer contributing to bonding, the hypothesis will be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use.
